context: Also used in scores and phone numbers. 'Zéro pointé' = a big fat zero.
'Un' before masculine nouns (un café), 'une' before feminine nouns (une pomme).
Before a vowel the x sounds like z: 'deux amis' [duh-zah-MEE].
Linking: 'trois enfants' [trwah-zahn-FAHN].
In fast speech often just [KAT].
The q is pronounced, except sometimes before a consonant: 'cinq livres' [san LEE-vruh].
Pronounced [SEE] before a consonant (six livres) and [SEEZ] before a vowel (six ans).
The p is silent.
No linking before huit: 'le huit' (not l'huit).
Becomes [nuhv] in 'neuf ans' and 'neuf heures'.
Same pattern as six: [DEE] before a consonant, [DEEZ] before a vowel.
No elision before onze: 'le onze novembre'.
'Une douzaine' = a dozen (of eggs, oysters…).
'Quinze jours' means two weeks in everyday French.
The last number with its own name. From 17: dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf.
Literally ten-seven. Same logic for dix-huit and dix-neuf.
The g and t are silent, except in 21–29: vingt-deux [vant-DUH].
21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71 use 'et': trente et un, soixante et onze.
Then quarante (40), cinquante (50), soixante (60).
The x sounds like s.
Literally sixty-ten: 71 = soixante et onze, 72 = soixante-douze… In Belgium and Switzerland: septante.
Literally four twenties. It takes an s only when nothing follows: quatre-vingt-un has no s.
Four twenties and ten: 99 = quatre-vingt-dix-neuf. Belgians and Swiss say nonante.
Never 'un cent'. Deux cents takes an s, but deux cent dix doesn't.
Never takes an s: deux mille, trois mille.
The polite, standard question. In speech: 'Il est quelle heure ?'

front: Il est trois heures et demie.
context: 'Et demie' = half past; 'et quart' = quarter past; 'moins le quart' = quarter to.
'Minuit' = midnight. Don't say 'douze heures' in conversation for noon (though it's correct in timetables).

front: Le train part à dix-huit heures trente.
pronunciation: [luh tran par ah dee-zwee tuhr TRAHNT]
context: France uses the 24-hour clock for timetables, appointments and official times.

front: À quelle heure ouvre la boulangerie ?
back: What time does the bakery open?
context: 'À quelle heure…?' = at what time…? 'Ferme' = closes.
Days of the week are masculine and written with a small letter. The week starts on Monday in France.
From Mars. 'Mardi gras' = Shrove Tuesday.
Primary schools often have no classes on Wednesday afternoon in France.
From Jupiter ('Jove').
From Venus.
'Le samedi' (with an article) = on Saturdays, every Saturday.
Many shops are closed on Sunday in France.
Months are masculine and written with a small letter: en janvier, au mois de janvier.
Then mars (March), avril (April), mai (May).
Don't confuse it with juillet (July) [zhwee-YEH].
'Le 14 juillet' (Bastille Day) is the national holiday.
Usually pronounced [OOT] (sometimes [OO]). Many French people go on holiday in August.
Then octobre, novembre, décembre.
Also: 'On est le combien aujourd'hui ?' (casual).
Only the first day uses an ordinal (le premier); after that: le deux mai, le trois mai.

front: Mon anniversaire, c'est le douze avril.
context: French dates go day-month-year: 12/04 = 12 April.

front: Je suis né en mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze.
pronunciation: [zhuh swee nay ahn meel nuhf sahn kah-truh-van-KANZ]
context: Years are read as full numbers: mil neuf cent… A woman writes 'née'.

front: Il y a quatre saisons : le printemps, l'été, l'automne et l'hiver.
pronunciation: [eel yah kah-truh seh-ZOHN: luh pran-TAHN, lay-TAY, loh-TUN ay lee-VEHR]
back: There are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter.
context: 'Au printemps' but 'en été, en automne, en hiver'.

front: Le rendez-vous est dans deux semaines.
back: The appointment is in two weeks.
context: 'Dans' + time = in (from now). 'Il y a deux semaines' = two weeks ago.
Prices: euros first, then cents, often without saying 'centimes'. Linking: 'vingt-cinq euros' [vant-san-kuh-ROH].
